But few were willing, or able, to dive into the Aruna who sat alone on her apartment balcony at three in the morning, staring at the city sky that never sleeps, with a glass of warm tea and a stack of philosophy books at her side. The Aruna who sometimes cried without clear reason, only because she felt too much or actually too little.

And then, there were those shadows. Scandal. One word that had once nearly destroyed everything, more than a decade ago. A youthful mistake, a negligence, a betrayal of trust that was recorded and spread without mercy. The virtual world had a feast, reviling, judging. She remembered how it felt to be at rock bottom, feeling there was no future anymore. At that time, she swore, if she managed to rise, she would build the highest possible fortress around her heart. And she succeeded. Her career skyrocketed again, even higher than before. But that fortress, that fortress remained standing sturdy. Too sturdy, perhaps.

That scandal taught her many things. About the fragility of privacy in the digital era. About who is a true friend and who is only there when you're triumphant. About the power of forgiving oneself, though the world might not necessarily forgive. But that wound, though it had dried, left a scar. A scar that made her extra careful, extra selective, even perhaps cynical toward sincerity.

“Sincerity,” Ara murmured that word while cleaning the remaining makeup from her face with cotton. Her real face began appearing. Pale, with faint circles under her eyes. “Does that still exist in this world? Or does it only exist in the lyrics of the songs I sing?”

She walked toward the large window in that dressing room. From that height, she could see the crowd of spectators beginning to disperse, like ants moving in order. Camera flashes from their phones were still occasionally visible, perhaps capturing remnants of euphoria. They would go home carrying tonight's memories. Carrying stories about Aruna the Diva who performed mesmerizingly.
But who would carry the story about Ara who now stood alone, behind the glitter, wondering whether anyone out there truly wanted to know her?
2: Compatibility. That was a word she often contemplated lately. Not merely compatibility of music or film taste. But compatibility of soul. Understanding each other without needing many words. Supporting each other without expecting return. Accepting each other, with all the inevitable strengths and weaknesses. Was that too lofty to ask?

At her current age, she no longer sought a Prince on a White Horse as in fairy tales. She also didn't need a man richer or more famous than her; that actually often became a source of new problems, exhausting veiled competition. She only wanted a partner. A life companion. Someone she could laugh freely with without pretense, someone whose shoulder was strong enough for her to lean on when the world felt too heavy, and conversely, she too wanted to become the same shelter for that person.
Ara let out a long sigh, then turned from the window. She reached for her phone again, this time opening the messaging app. There was a message from Vera.
“Hotel is secure. No media can get through. You can rest. Tomorrow at 10 AM we'll discuss the new single's release schedule.”
Ara typed a brief reply: “Okay, Ver. Thanks.”

She looked again at her reflection in the mirror. The woman there looked more fragile now, without stage lights disguising everything. But in her eyes, there was a flash of determination. Tired, yes. Empty, sometimes. But giving up? No. Aruna Candrakirana was never taught to give up.

Maybe, she thought, maybe out there, among seven billion humans, there's one soul also searching. One soul whose frequency is the same. One soul who won't run seeing her fortress, but rather patiently seek its gate, or even, help Ara find that gate's key which she might have long forgotten where she stored.

That thought gave her a little warmth. A little hope. Enough to make her step toward the bathroom, cleanse herself of the remnants of stage grandeur, and prepare herself to welcome tomorrow. A tomorrow that might just, somehow, bring her closer to what her heart truly missed. No longer applause, no longer trophies. But a sincere handhold, amid the noise and silence of life. A place where her tired soul could finally truly come home.

She turned off the dressing room's main light, leaving one table lamp glowing dimly. In that dim light, Aruna Candrakirana, the diva, temporarily disappeared. What remained was only Ara, a woman longing for genuine connection, amid the magnificent stage of her life that sometimes felt so lonely.

Ara came out of the bathroom an hour later, her body feeling fresher after soaking in warm water with lavender aroma. Her wet black hair hung down her back, wrapped in a thick towel. She wore ivory silk pajamas, her most comfortable clothing contrasting with her all-glittering stage costumes. That room was still silent. She glanced at the digital clock on the nightstand. Almost two in the morning.

She walked toward the minibar, not to take an alcoholic drink as many people might imagine about a rock star post-concert. She took a bottle of cold mineral water and a small box of her favorite dark chocolate. Bittersweet just right, like her life.

While chewing a piece of chocolate, Ara opened her laptop. Not to check work emails or social media. She opened a folder containing drafts of unfinished songs, raw melodies that often came at unexpected moments. Her fingers moved nimbly over the keyboard, not typing lyrics, but playing several chord progressions on music software. This was her other escape. Creating. Here she could be herself, pouring out all her restlessness and hope without filter.

Several melodies sounded melancholic, reflecting her mood tonight. There were also ones with an optimistic nuance, as if her deepest soul refused to surrender to emptiness. She often wondered, could her music's enjoyers truly feel what she tried to convey behind those poetic lyrics and magnificent arrangements? Or did they only enjoy its surface, its melody's beauty, her voice's sweetness?
Once, in the early days of her relationships with several men, she often played her most personal compositions. Hoping they could “hear” more than merely notes.
They didn't understand. They didn't want to understand. Or maybe she hoped too much.

That fortress, she realized, wasn't only built by past scandal. That fortress was also built by piles of disappointment from failed relationships, from unfulfilled expectations, from the feeling that she always had to be “Aruna the Diva,” even in her most private space. When could she just be “Ara”?

She remembered her father, a simple music teacher in a small town in Central Java. Her father was the first person to see her talent, who taught her her first musical notes, who patiently listened to her singing off-key in childhood.

“That voice is a gift, Nduk,” her father said one afternoon, while fixing his old guitar strings. “But more important than a voice's sweetness is what you want to convey through that voice. Your heart's honesty.”

Heart's honesty. Ironically, the higher her stage, the harder it was for her to find room for that purest heart's honesty. Everything had to be measured, calculated. Every performance, every interview, even every social media post, had to pass management team consideration. For the sake of “image.” For the sake of “brand.”
Ara closed her laptop. Tonight, inspiration felt blocked. Maybe because her energy had been drained on stage. Or maybe because her heart was too full of questions without answers yet.

She walked toward the large window once more. The city below still glowed though not as busy as a few hours ago. She imagined Bima, that rising young actor, whom she'd met several times at award events or commercial shoot locations. She remembered Bima's different gaze. Not a blindly worshipping gaze, nor an opportunistic gaze full of calculation. There was a kind of sincere curiosity there, there was respect that felt natural. They had once been involved in a brief conversation backstage at a television program. About books, about independent films, about meaning behind a work. A conversation that surprised Ara because of its depth, amid the bustle of live broadcast preparation.

“Someone like him,” Ara thought, “is he one of those who can still see beyond the facade?” But that thought she immediately dismissed. Too early. Too many bad “what ifs” she had experienced. Bima might just be the same as the others, only better at playing a role at the beginning. Or maybe, Ara herself was already too tired to even merely hope.

Suddenly, her phone rang. This time not a message notification, but an incoming call. Vera's name appeared on the screen. Ara furrowed her brow. Unusual for Vera to call this late after ensuring everything was secure.
“Yes, Ver? What is it?” Ara answered, trying to make her voice not sound too tired.

“Sorry to disturb so late, Ra. But this is somewhat important and I just got its confirmation,” Vera's voice sounded serious. “Remember about the musical film collaboration project with director Adi Pratama we once discussed in passing?”
Ara tried to remember. So many projects discussed in passing. “Which one? The folktale adaptation?”

“No, this one is new. Contemporary romantic drama. They've finalized the script, and the female lead role was indeed written with you in mind. The producer called earlier, they want to meet as soon as possible for a presentation.”
Ara fell silent a moment. A new project again. New busyness again. “I thought I wanted a little pause after this tour, Ver.”
“I know, Ra. But this is a big project. Its male lead… they're targeting Bima Prawira.”
That name, mentioned again tonight, made Ara stunned momentarily. Bima Prawira. The actor who had earlier crossed her mind. What kind of coincidence was this?
“Bima?” Ara repeated, more to herself.
“Yes. They say your chemistry when you were guest stars on that talkshow was really good. Many fans liked it. So the producer feels you're a fitting couple on screen.”

Ara felt slight irony. Chemistry on screen. This industry was indeed expert at creating illusion. But somehow, there was a bit of curiosity stirred. Working together with Bima on a film project. That would mean there'd be lots of interaction, lots of time to see further behind his public charm. Was this an opportunity? Or actually a new test for her heart's fortress?
“What do you think, Ra?” Vera asked, breaking her daydream. “If you're interested, I can schedule the meeting for the day after tomorrow.”
Ara looked out the window again. The city lights now looked like stars fallen to earth. Distant, cold, yet still radiating faint beauty.
“Okay, Ver,” Ara answered after a pause of several seconds. Her voice sounded steadier than she'd expected. “Just arrange the meeting. Let's see what it's like first.”
“Great! I'll inform you of the details tomorrow. Rest, Ra. You deserve quality rest.”
“You too, Ver. Good night.”

The call ended. Ara set down her phone. Silence again enveloped the room, but this time it felt slightly different. There was a glimmer of anticipation, though she tried to suppress it. Bima Prawira. A new film project. Somehow, the night that had earlier felt so long and empty, now had a new focal point in the distance.

She didn't know what would happen. She didn't know whether this would become the next disappointment, or something… different. But for the first time that night, there was a slight sincere smile etched on Aruna Candrakirana's lips. Not a smile for the camera, not a smile for the audience. A smile for herself. A smile carrying a sliver of hope amid her magnificent stage that often felt lonely, that maybe just, her tired soul would find something that could make her feel whole again.
Maybe.
3: Far from the glitter of the magnificent stadium and camera flashes that last night embraced Aruna Candrakirana, a simple apartment in South Jakarta's corner became a silent witness to the beginning of a new day. Morning sunlight, which managed to slip through gray curtain gaps, fell right on a pile of books and drama scripts scattered on an old teak wooden table. Beside it, a cup of green tea with only a quarter left looked already cold. On the also-gray sofa, lay Bima Prawira, still asleep with soft snoring.

There was no conspicuous luxury in that two-bedroom apartment. Its walls were decorated with several classic independent film posters, an abstract painting by his not-yet-famous friend, and a tall bookshelf packed full, its contents ranging from literary novels, biographies of inspirational figures, to acting theory books. Everything reflected its occupant's personality: a thirty-two-year-old man who valued substance over appearance, depth over mere popularity.

Bima stretched slowly, his eyes blinking adjusting to the light. He reached for the phone on the small table beside the sofa, looking at the time. Half past seven in the morning. Last night he'd stayed up, not to party, but to study the script for his newest film, a supporting role, but with a complex and challenging character. For him, a role's size was never the main issue. What mattered was how that role could give him room to explore, to dig into another side of his humanity.

After a simple morning ritual — washing his face, brushing his teeth, and brewing a cup of strong black coffee — Bima sat on his small balcony facing the bustle of Jakarta's streets beginning to stir. Morning air still felt fresh, though city pollution was already thinly felt in the nose. He opened a book on Stoic philosophy, one of his favorite readings lately. Seeking tranquility and wisdom amid an entertainment industry that often felt like an emotional roller coaster.

Bima Prawira. His name had begun being widely known in the last five years. Several films he starred in managed to achieve commercial success and critical praise. His photogenic face with a shady yet sharp gaze often appeared in magazines and television programs. He had a loyal fan base, who appreciated his natural acting talent and his personality that seemed humble. Quite famous, yes. Established enough to live comfortably, of course. But he was aware, he wasn't yet in Aruna Candrakirana's league.

Aruna. That name sometimes crossed his mind, especially after their brief meeting a few months ago at a talkshow event. He remembered well how that woman, who from afar looked so majestic and untouchable, turned out to have a crisp laugh and intelligent questions when they chatted briefly backstage. There was a fragility briefly caught in her eyes, something that made Bima feel that behind her diva image, there was an ordinary human who might also feel the things he felt.

Bima never had ambition to become the “brightest star.” The nickname “The Dimly Shining Star” once bestowed by a senior journalist in a review of his film actually felt more fitting for him. Dim didn't mean without light, but rather its light wasn't blinding, was shading, and invited people to look closer, deeper. He wanted to be known for his work, for his acting quality, not for sensation or his private life exposed thoroughly.

This principle was what made him often reject tempting offers not aligned with his idealism. He had once rejected becoming a model for a product advertisement whose efficacy he himself didn't believe in though its fee was sky-high. He had also withdrawn from a big film project because he felt its scenario was shallow and only sold cheap sensuality. Decisions like that sometimes made him disagree with his manager, Doni, who was more pragmatic.
